title: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species are not independently created and immutable; species of the same genus are lineal descendants of some other, generally extinct, species, just as varieties of one species descend from that species.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I am fully convinced that species are not immutable; but that those belonging to what are called the same genera are lineal descendants of some other and generally extinct species, in the same manner as the acknowledged varieties of any one species are the descendants of that species.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), the Introduction; section “Introduction”. Scope: all species of plants and animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-intro-04: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.80

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Multiple large public resources contain independent molecular and fossil consequences of descent. Although complete species coverage is absent, the universal immutability alternative has clear, strongly discriminating tests.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare independent molecular characters, shared derived genomic changes and fossil succession against separate-creation and common-descent models. Nested congruent ancestry across congeneric species supports descent; independent origins without shared history would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Fossil ancestors are rarely identifiable with certainty.

Not every described species has genomic data.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.91
discriminating power: 0.83
operationalizability: 0.78
analysis feasibility: 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public sequences, a synthetic tree, and fossil occurrences already contain the variables needed to test shared ancestry and extinct stems for a large fraction of named plant and animal genera. Concordance across loci and fossils keeps the test from simply assuming the tree that classification built. Coverage is incomplete, especially outside vertebrates and vascular plants, but it is broad enough that a standard comparative analysis could confirm or refute the generalization rather than only a narrow proxy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Test whether species placed in the same genus form clades on sequence data, using concordance across independent loci rather than a single assumed tree, and whether the inferred ancestral node is older than the living members and matched by extinct fossil relatives. Independent creation or immutability would be favoured if genetic similarity were not hierarchically nested or if living species were routinely ancestral to their congeners; shared ancestry from earlier, now extinct lineages would favour the historical claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Genus limits are themselves revised using phylogenies, so a test must freeze a pre-molecular classification or use rank-free clades.

Many named genera still lack sequence data, and the fossil record is sparse for soft-bodied groups and plants.

Hybrid speciation and incomplete lineage sorting produce local non-monophyly without restoring independent creation.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.8
analysis feasibility: 0.76
data existence: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.66
